summary.text: The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799.
Financial crisis and widespread social distress led to the Estates General meeting in May 1789, its first meeting since 1614.
Many of its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and its values remain central to modern French political discourse.

items.prompt: The nobility and Church had many tax exemptions in 18th-century France. Who ended up paying most of the tax?

options.label: The merchants alone
The lower classes
The king's ministers
The regional Parlements

items.explain: Because the nobility and Church benefited from exemptions, the tax burden fell mainly on the lower classes.

items.prompt: Under the old format for the Estates-General, each estate voted as a bloc. Why did that hurt the Third Estate?

options.label: The Third Estate was barred from speaking to the king in meetings
The Third Estate had to pay for the whole meeting by itself
The clergy and nobility could combine to outvote it despite being under 5% of the population
The Third Estate was allowed only one representative in total

items.explain: Votes were counted by estate rather than by head, so the clergy and nobility could outvote the Third Estate.

items.prompt: Finance minister Calonne proposed a universal land tax and other reforms. What happened to them?

options.label: The Assembly of Notables and then the parlements refused, saying only an Estates-General could approve them
The king passed them by decree, and the nobility accepted the new taxes without any protest at all
The Third Estate approved them in a vote, and the reforms took effect across the kingdom at once
Calonne withdrew them himself after the people of Paris rioted against the new land tax in the streets

items.explain: The new taxes were rejected, and the notables and parlements argued that only an Estates-General could approve them.

items.prompt: After another revolt in June 1793 and the suspension of the constitution, political power passed from the National Convention to which body?

options.label: The Directory, led by Napoleon Bonaparte
The Estates General, called by the king
The Assembly of Notables, hand-picked by Calonne
The Committee of Public Safety, dominated by radical Jacobins

items.explain: Power passed to the Committee of Public Safety, dominated by radical Jacobins led by Robespierre.

items.prompt: In the 1780s educated French people debated liberty, equality and democracy. What helped inspire that debate?

options.label: The decision of the king to give up his throne
Enlightenment critiques and the American Revolution
The spread of Catholic Church control over the state
A war to take back territory from Britain

items.explain: Enlightenment critiques of institutions and the American Revolution inspired public debate on patriotism, liberty, equality and democracy.

items.prompt: What brought the unstable Directory to an end?

options.label: The execution of Louis XVI, which set up a new republic
The revolt of June, which gave power to the Convention
The coup of 18 Brumaire, which set up the Consulate with Napoleon as First Consul
The Thermidorian Reaction, which put Robespierre in charge

items.explain: The Directory's instability ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire and the establishment of the Consulate with Napoleon as First Consul.

paragraphs.heading: A decade that remade France
paragraphs.text: The French Revolution was a stretch of political and social upheaval in France. It opened with the Estates General of 1789 and closed on 9 November 1799 with the Coup of 18 Brumaire. Many of its ideas are seen as core principles of liberal democracy. Its values are still at the center of political debate in France today.

paragraphs.heading: Money troubles
paragraphs.text: Through the 1700s, France kept running into budget crises because its spending grew faster than its income. The economy grew, but because the state relied on tax farmers, its tax income did not rise in step. Tax rates differed from region to region and were gathered unevenly, and because nobles and the Church enjoyed many exemptions, the burden landed mostly on the lower classes. France paid for its 1778 to 1783 war with Britain mainly with loans, and by 1788 half of the state's revenue went on servicing its debt.

paragraphs.heading: Hard times and new ideas
paragraphs.text: France's population rose from 21 to 28 million between 1715 and 1789. Overall prosperity grew, but its gains stayed mostly with the rentier and merchant classes, while living standards fell for wage workers and peasants who rented land. A slump from 1785 and poor harvests in 1787 and 1788 pushed up unemployment and food prices. Meanwhile educated people debated Enlightenment criticism of society, and the American Revolution stirred talk of liberty, equality and democracy.

paragraphs.heading: Reform blocked
paragraphs.text: New tax laws had to be registered with regional courts called parlements, and these could block them. In 1786 the finance minister, Calonne, proposed reforms including a single land tax paid by all. An Assembly of Notables, dominated by nobles, rejected the new taxes, and so did the parlements. They insisted only an Estates-General could approve such taxes, a representative body that had last met in 1614. In August 1788, after failing to raise new loans, the government announced that the king would call one for the following May.

paragraphs.heading: The Third Estate breaks away
paragraphs.text: The Estates-General was split into three estates: the clergy, the nobility, and the commoners, known as the Third Estate. Votes were counted by estate, so the clergy and nobility, less than 5% of the people, could outvote the commoners. In June 1789, the Third Estate's representatives broke away and named themselves a National Assembly. On 14 July the Bastille in Paris was stormed, and in the wake of that event the Assembly abolished feudalism, put the Catholic Church under state control, and issued a Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen.

paragraphs.heading: From monarchy to republic
paragraphs.text: Three years of struggle for political control followed. In June 1791 King Louis XVI attempted to flee, an episode known as the flight to Varennes, and this damaged the monarchy further, and military defeats after war broke out in April 1792 led to an uprising on 10 August 1792. In September the monarchy was replaced by the French First Republic, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.

paragraphs.heading: Terror and its end
paragraphs.text: A further revolt in June 1793 led to the constitution being set aside, and power moved to the Committee of Public Safety, a body controlled by radical Jacobins whose leader was Maximilien Robespierre. In the Reign of Terror, about 16,000 people were condemned by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed. The Terror ended in July 1794 with the Thermidorian Reaction. In November 1795 a government called the Directory took over, and its unstable rule ended in 1799 when Napoleon Bonaparte became First Consul.
